title: Level 3 – Global Nurse Professional
subtitle: Mother and Newborn Care
intro: Supporting Mothers and Newborns Welcome to the highest level of the GNPS learning pathway. Global Nursing Professionals improve maternal and newborn outcomes beyond the individual bedside. They lead safety initiatives, strengthen referral systems, mentor staff, use data and support equitable access to respectful maternity care. This level develops advanced capability in maternal-newborn leadership, perinatal quality improvement, clinical governance, evidence translation, digital maternity care, workforce development and global maternal and neonatal health. Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: Lead respectful and safe maternity services Strengthen systems for recognising maternal and neonatal deterioration Analyse maternal and neonatal outcomes and near misses Design and evaluate quality-improvement initiatives Promote evidence-based perinatal practice Support equitable access and culturally safe care Use digital maternity technologies responsibly Mentor teams in clinical judgement and emergency response Contribute to global maternal and newborn health improvement Preventable maternal and newborn harm often reflects system weaknesses such as delayed referral, limited resources, poor communication, inconsistent monitoring or inequitable access. Global Nursing Professionals recognise these connections and lead practical improvements. By completing Level 3, you should be prepared to lead maternity and newborn quality initiatives, use evidence and data to improve systems, support colleagues and contribute to healthier beginnings locally and globally.

sections.title: Leading Respectful and Safe Maternity Services

content.text: Leadership in maternal and newborn care means creating services where women and families are treated with dignity, staff can raise concerns and evidence-based care is available reliably. Global Nursing Professionals model respectful practice and strengthen clinical governance.
Learning outcomes
Describe leadership responsibilities in maternity services Promote respectful and psychologically safe care
Support staff competence and emergency readiness Strengthen clinical governance and accountability

Respectful Maternity Care Women should receive privacy, dignity, informed choice and freedom from discrimination or mistreatment. Respectful care is a safety issue as well as an ethical responsibility.
Psychological Safety Staff need confidence to question abnormal findings, request help and report near misses without humiliation. This supports early intervention.
Competence and Simulation Regular education, drills and team simulation strengthen response to haemorrhage, eclampsia, shoulder dystocia and neonatal resuscitation.
Clinical Governance Policies, audit, credentialing, incident review and outcome monitoring provide oversight and support consistent practice.

A maternity unit identifies that junior staff hesitate to activate the emergency team. Leaders introduce multidisciplinary simulation, clear escalation criteria and supportive debriefing. Activation becomes earlier and staff confidence improves.
Key learning points
Make respectful care a measurable standard Create a culture where concerns are heard
Use simulation to build team readiness Link policy with visible leadership and accountability

sections.title: Improving Maternal and Neonatal Safety Systems

content.text: Preventable maternal and newborn harm often involves delayed recognition, communication failure or weak referral pathways. Systems thinking helps leaders understand how work conditions influence outcomes.
Learning outcomes
Analyse maternal and neonatal incidents using systems thinking Strengthen escalation and referral pathways
Use maternal and perinatal review to support learning Recommend practical risk controls
Deterioration Systems Maternal early warning tools and neonatal observation pathways can support recognition, but they must be completed accurately and linked to timely response.
Referral and Transfer Clear criteria, communication channels, transport arrangements and receiving-team coordination are essential, especially in rural or resource-limited settings.
Review of Serious Events Maternal death, severe morbidity, stillbirth and neonatal deterioration should be reviewed respectfully to identify clinical and system learning.
Human Factors Workload, fatigue, hierarchy, equipment layout and unclear roles can contribute to missed deterioration. Stronger controls redesign the system rather than relying only on reminders.

A review of delayed postpartum haemorrhage responses finds inconsistent emergency equipment and uncertainty about team roles. The service standardises trolleys, introduces role cards and runs regular drills. Response times and treatment reliability improve.
Key learning points
Look beyond individual blame Strengthen the connection between monitoring and response
Standardise critical equipment and roles Use serious-event review to drive measurable change
Global Nursing Professionals use data and evidence to improve antenatal, intrapartum, postnatal and newborn outcomes. Improvement should be specific, practical and evaluated over time.
Learning outcomes
Use outcome data to identify priorities Apply structured quality-improvement methods
Translate evidence into practical maternity care Evaluate patient experience and equity
Choosing Improvement Priorities Possible priorities include maternal hypertension, haemorrhage, infection, breastfeeding support, preterm birth, newborn hypothermia or delayed referral.
Testing Change Teams define the problem, map current practice, test a focused change and study results before wider implementation.
Evidence Translation Guidelines should be converted into usable pathways, education, equipment and documentation rather than remaining as policy documents alone.
Measurement and Equity Outcome, process and balancing measures should be reviewed across different populations to identify unequal access or outcomes.

A service identifies high newborn hypothermia rates. The team introduces immediate drying, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact, warm transport and temperature documentation. Rates improve, and the team also checks that the pathway is applied consistently across all birth settings.
Key learning points
Define the problem before selecting the solution Translate evidence into reliable workflow
Measure outcomes and unintended effects Examine whether improvement benefits all families

sections.title: Digital Maternity Care and Global Maternal-Newborn Health

content.text: Digital records, remote monitoring, telehealth and decision-support tools can improve maternity care, but they can also create privacy, access and automation risks. Global Nursing Professionals use technology critically while addressing wider maternal and newborn inequities.
Learning outcomes
Evaluate digital tools used in maternity care Recognise technology-related risks and inequity
Support integrated care across services Contribute to global maternal and neonatal improvement
Digital Maternity Records Shared electronic records can improve continuity, but incorrect or incomplete data may create false confidence. Critical information must be verified.

Remote and Rural Care Telehealth and remote monitoring can extend antenatal and postnatal support, provided that clear escalation pathways and alternatives for people without digital access are available.

Decision Support and Automation Electronic alerts and fetal-monitoring technologies may assist clinicians but do not replace professional assessment. Alert fatigue and automation bias require attention.
Global Health and Equity Reducing maternal and neonatal mortality requires skilled care, timely referral, essential medicines, respectful services and attention to social and geographic barriers.

A regional service introduces telehealth for high-risk antenatal follow-up. Leaders identify that some women have limited internet access and arrange community-based monitoring and telephone support. Technology expands care without excluding vulnerable families.
Key learning points
Use technology to support, not replace, clinical judgement Plan for privacy, downtime and digital exclusion
Coordinate maternity care across organisational boundaries Adapt global evidence to local resources and community needs

End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 6 - Level 3, you have developed the advanced perspective of a Global Nursing Professional. You are prepared not only to support mothers and newborns safely but also to lead respectful services, strengthen emergency systems, translate evidence, improve outcomes and contribute to equitable maternal and newborn healthcare.
GNPS Learning Pathway Level 1 - Qualified Nurse: Build strong foundations in pregnancy, labour, postnatal and newborn care.
Level 2 - International Qualified Nurse: Manage high-risk maternity and neonatal care within international systems.
Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional: Lead quality, safety, equity and innovation in maternal-newborn services.
